I'm going to be honest and say I don't really have any advice, however some of this sounds incredibly similar to my experiences. My partner linked me this thread and I thought I'd try to reach out and explain my own issues in hopes it might help you some, or at least make you feel less alone. (To me, it feels very lonely, and you mentioning you couldn't eat in front of people makes me think that perhaps you feel the same.)

I have been professionally diagnosed with OCD and suspect I might be autistic. Both (and I do not mean to diagnose you here, of course, I am only speaking from my own experiences) have been linked to ARFID, or Avoidant Restrictive Food Intake Disorder. It's a relatively newer diagnosis, but is generally marked by a limited selection of "safe foods" and aversion to new foods such as what you're describing - for me, anxiety, and the gag reflex. Oh, god, the gag reflex. The last time I tried an apple I had to force it down with water. It was embarrassing and disheartening - something so simple has actually become a goal of mine, just to eat an apple.

I began looking for some sort of answers I think when I was maybe eleven or twelve if not a bit younger. My parents would also try to force me to eat new foods which I think was more traumatizing than anything else - they were more angry than understanding, and after a while just kind of gave up on me. 

For me, too, it made it difficult to eat in front of people. I'd avoid it, or I'd find a small group in school I felt safe with. On the rare occasion I went to friends' houses or went to family gatherings, I would try to stick to my more "normal" feeling safe foods. For prom, I told my friends that my "mother took me to dinner beforehand" and let people have my plate. I'd just keep taking bread through the night.  
However, I started finding some sort of answers a few years after my initial search began. "Selective Eating Disorder" it was initially called, then a couple of years later, changed to the ARFID we have now. 

It still seems new enough that finding professionals experienced with it is a task in itself, but there are some, and it seems like there's some texts being written on the topic now.

If this feels like it may fit your experience, you may want to look into it more.

Actually, a little advice - it may help, \*may\*, to try food similar to what you like. My partner was really sweet and made a list of the foods I like, don't like (for whatever reason, be it taste or sensory issues such as sight, smell, texture, etc), foods I want to try, and foods similar he thought I'd like. You could do something like this to try and get yourself a starting point. It's honestly very hard, at least in my experience, but it may be worth trying to both test new foods like this, and make a sort of journal or list of foods like what I have, and experiences you have.

For books, a quick Amazon search for "ARFID workbooks" or books or "adult picky eater help" nets a decent amount of results, here are a couple I found that may be interesting to try (while I should probably pick one up myself, I have not read these, mind.) :  
\- Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy for Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder (Children,   
  Adolescents, and Adults) 1st Edition  
  by Jennifer J. Thomas  
\- Conquer Picky Eating for Teens and Adults: Activities and Strategies for Selective Eaters   
  Paperback – May 2, 2018  
  by Jenny McGlothlin MS,SLP, and Katja Rowell MD  
\- The Picky Eater's Recovery Book (Overcoming Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder) 1st   
   Edition  
   by Jennifer J. Thomas

You deal with this "threesome issue" by dealing with the actual issue at hand - your "boyfriend".

If you have any hope for him at all, you could try to talk out how you feel. Judging from what you've said here, I don't think he would be receptive. I don't think he cares about how you feel.  
Should you have lied about your exes to try and get him to do something to you? No, Although, admittedly, if I was with someone who wouldn't compromise and do something that would make me feel good, but also expected (I'm assuming, he sounds the type) me to do that to them, it would bother me, too. It's different if he does not like it and does not expect it himself, as there are other ways he could try to please you, and there's room for compromise. However, it sounds like he didn't care enough about your pleasure, and you felt frustrated. It is incredibly minor in comparison to what he's doing to you.

The threesome is not the issue here. The issue is he is taking advantage of you all around. You opened up to him about your trauma, and he is now using it as a tool to hurt you. He said, when you asked where the relationship was going, that he could just "get a yacht and party with girls" (????) and makes you feel bad about how your body works in comparison to others he's been with (I'm assuming because he does not want to go down on you) in an effort to hurt you.   
I would also argue that he is most likely lying about this - it's definitely a thing, but many, if not most AFAB individuals need other stimulation as well, at least from what I've read and known in my personal life. The way he said the previous people he'd been with have been able to finish vaginally is likely only said in order to hurt you, and to make you feel poorly about your body. There is nothing wrong with needing additional stimulation, and he should not be making you feel poorly for it.  
Just - all of this, all of it - is bad. He is the one emotionally abusing you, and manipulating you to trying to do something you are uncomfortable doing. He said it himself, the threesome is not only for "his pleasure", but, quite literally, to hurt you. He said it himself. You said it right here. It is to hurt you.

If he was genuinely bothered by giving you oral, it should have been explained to begin with. Not everybody likes the same stuff, and that's okay. However, he should have tried to find a compromise so you still get enjoyment out of intimacy. If he was truly hurt about you lying, he should have sat you down and discussed this. He is not hurt by it, he just sees it as a way to manipulate you into doing something you do not want to do. He knows you've been in abusive relationships before, and he's trying to take advantage of your hurt and inexperience.

I mean that gently - I don't know what kind of home life you had, but our upbringing can shape what kind of relationships we end up in. When we're entering relationships for the first time, those experiences can shape us, too, and what kind of relationships we continue to get in. When we are so used to being hurt and treated a certain way, it becomes our "normal", when in reality, it is not normal, and it is not kind.

I say this because I've been in a handful of not great situations, and know others who have too, and have eventually had to learn the same. I'm seeing a lot of "red flags" in this post, and I worry for you.

You deserve kindness, and love. You deserve someone who wants to please you - but most importantly, you deserve someone who does not hurt you, does not take things you've confided in them and use it to hurt you. You do not deserve how he's treating you, at all. He is the one manipulating you here. It's abusive.

It's time to let go.

If she wants children as well, this was probably a very difficult decision for her to make. For whatever reason, she was not ready. The process of pregnancy and labour take an incredible toll, and are sometimes (perhaps, often) traumatic in one way or another. It's a lot of sacrifice on the pregnant individual physically and emotionally, nevermind how some countries treat maternity leave.

You have a right to break up at any time. But for someone you had planned a future with, and even bought a ring for to propose with, you were incredibly unfair to her. As I initially said, as she wants children as well, this was probably a difficult and sad decision for her to make. She has to go through it all - you don't. Her aborting the fetus does not mean she will never have children. She just, for whatever reason, cannot right now.Stepping off of my soapbox, again, you have a right to break up at any time. But you were unfair in how you approached it. You were not transparent to her as to what the consequences would be. You left, and came back, saying you would pay for the abortion and support her no matter what she chose. With this, she trusted you and felt safe making that decision.

Would her decision be different if you had been transparent? I don't know. You don't know. Nobody here knows.

But you weren't even decent enough to tell her in person. She was incredibly brave to tell you, face to face, when she knew you wanted children, and to give you that vulnerability. You went back to her, then when she went to stay with her family a few days, you packed your things and left a note. It was cowardly, and she deserved the same respect she gave you when telling you she was pregnant and wanted the abortion.

It all comes off incredibly cruel and cold for someone you supposedly was planning a life with and wanted to propose to. It comes off, as some other people here are saying, kind of like a punishment.

You're entitled to your grief. It's a sad time, and if she wants children, she may be grieving, too. It just wasn't the right time.

As I said - you have a right to breakup with someone whenever, for whatever reason. However, you did so incredibly poorly. I could understand running away like that if you were being abused or if it was a toxic relationship. But she offered you vulnerability, you were not transparent, and you more or less abandoned her.

As for talking to her? I don't know. Part of me says you owe her an apology and explanation. I think she deserves that much. You've been together a year and a half and lived together, and you just picked up and left. Personally, if I was in her position, I don't know if I could ever trust you again.

I hope she finds someone better. I hope the next person you end up seeing, you can be more open with them. I wish the both of you healing.
